title: Committed default FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY defeats at-rest field encryption
rationale:
Root cause is two-layered. The cited sink (docker-compose-prod-postgres.yml:86) supplies a world-known Fernet key via the `${SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY:-DtlkqVb3...=}` fallback, so a no-op `docker compose up` runs with a public key. But the deeper root cause is `backend/config/settings/base.py:432`, which read `env("FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY")` with no validation — THREAT_MODEL.md:112 lists exactly this fail-closed boot check as a still-missing control, and many other files (helm chart, dev compose, CI scripts) also carry the same key.

Fix at both layers, smallest change each:
- Compose: swap `:-default` for `:?error` so an unset `SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` makes compose abort with a pointer to the key-generation docs, instead of silently substituting the burned key. No literal secret remains in the cited file.
- Code (the true root cause): `base.py:432` now routes the value through a new pure helper `validate_field_encryption_key`, which raises `ImproperlyConfigured` if the key is empty or equals any known-burned default. This enforces fail-closed regardless of which deployment path (compose, helm, manual env, .env) supplied the value, so it catches the variants the compose-only edit cannot. The helper lives in `application/commons/services/settings_validation.py` with zero Django-model imports so it is safe to import at settings-load time.
variants_checked: Grepped `FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` / `DtlkqVb3wlaVdJK` across the repo. Sibling injection sites carrying the same burned key: docker-compose-prod-mysql.yml:86, docker-compose-prod-test.yml:53, docker-compose-dev.yml:41, docker-compose-dev-mysql.yml:41, docker-compose-dev-keycloak.yml:50, docker-compose-playwright.yml:47, docker-compose-unittests.yml:20, docker/backend/unittests/envs/django:15, backend/bin/run_pylint.sh:19, backend/bin/run_mypy.sh:19, charts/secobserve/values.yaml:173. Consumer: config/settings/base.py:432 (single read point). I did not edit the dev/test/CI/unittest files or the helm chart: those are intentionally-static test fixtures or operator-supplied secret references, and the `base.py` fail-closed check now defends every production boot path centrally. The gitleaks parser fixtures and TRIAGE/VULN/THREAT_MODEL docs that mention the key are reporting artifacts, not config, and were left untouched.
bypass_considered: Attacker variation: set `SO_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEY` to the burned key explicitly (the compose `:?` only catches *unset*, not a deliberately-supplied bad value), or supply it via helm/`.env`/manual `-e`. The compose-only edit would not stop this. The `base.py` helper does: it checks the resolved value against `BURNED_FIELD_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` and raises regardless of source, so every path that ends at `base.py:432` fails closed. Residual gap: a different but still public key not in the burned set would pass — addressed by documenting per-deployment key generation rather than enumerable blocklisting; entropy validation of an arbitrary key is out of scope for this finding.
test_note: Added backend/unittests/commons/services/test_settings_validation.py (alongside the existing commons/services tests). It uses `django.test.SimpleTestCase` (no DB) since the helper is pure. `test_burned_default_key_rejected` and `test_empty_key_rejected` fail before the change (no helper / no validation) and pass after; `test_fresh_key_accepted` guards against over-blocking. A direct test of `base.py`'s module-level raise was avoided because the settings module imports at suite startup with the burned key still in the unittest env, which would break the whole run — hence the extracted, independently-testable helper.
review_reason: The core approach is correct and root-cause (compose line 86 made mandatory via `:?`, and `base.py:432` now fail-closes through `validate_field_encryption_key`, matching the existing `raise ValueError` style at base.py:437-438), and it adds no new attack surface. But it is incomplete and regresses tests: `unittests.py`→`prod.py`→`base.py` runs the new burned-key check, while the test/CI environments still feed that exact key (`docker/backend/unittests/envs/django:15`, `docker-compose-unittests.yml:20`, `run_pylint.sh:19`, `run_mypy.sh:19`), so settings import will raise ImproperlyConfigured and break the suite, pylint, and mypy. It also only patches one of the shipped compose files — the identical default still lives in `docker-compose-prod-mysql.yml:86` and `docker-compose-prod-test.yml:53`, leaving the vulnerability active in sibling production artifacts.
